title: La Jara Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: La Jara wells have a 120 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $12,000-$21,000.
h1: La Jara, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near La Jara means looking closely at the local well record, not relying on a countywide average. Within five miles of La Jara, Colorado DWR records include 1,315 permitted wells. Of those, 1,012 are recorded as constructed, 1,037 report total depth, 151 report pump yield, and 85 report static water level.

The local picture is generally favorable: the median well is 120 feet deep, the median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the median static water level is 8 feet below the surface. Those figures are useful for planning, but a neighboring well is still the best starting point for a property-specific investigation.

sections.heading: What La Jara well depths look like
sections.html:
La Jara wells have a median reported depth of 120 feet. The middle half runs from 90 to 200 feet, meaning many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow well, while still allowing for variation from lot to lot. About 27% of reported wells are under 100 feet, and 58% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Depths become less typical above that range. About 10% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 5% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record reaches 4,000 feet. Local permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers on 749 wells and the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer systems on 497 wells combined. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can make the actual drilling conditions change over a short distance.

sections.heading: How much water a La Jara well may produce
sections.html:
The reported median yield near La Jara is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is weighted toward stronger results: 58% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 40% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield wells are uncommon in the available records, but they are not impossible. About 1% report less than 1 gallon per minute, and another 1% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Only 151 wells report a pump yield, so treat the percentages as a useful local signal rather than a guarantee. Ask for the well test, permitted use, storage setup, and any production problems before assuming a property can support a home, livestock, or irrigation.

sections.heading: La Jara water levels and recent measurements
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow in this area. The median depth to water is 8 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 1 to 12 feet. That matters during construction because shallow groundwater can affect excavation, trenching, basement planning, and wellhead protection.

The available decade comparison does not show a dropping trend. The median static water level was 10 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Only 85 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited record rather than a complete groundwater study. A buyer should compare the subject well with nearby permits in La Jara, Sanford, Manassa, Romeo, and Capulin, then confirm current conditions with a well professional.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around La Jara, and how old are the permits
sections.html:
Permit history shows sustained well construction around La Jara rather than a single short period of activity. The records include 73 permits from the 1950s, 26 from the 1960s, 251 from the 1970s, 49 from the 1980s, 108 from the 1990s, 245 from the 2000s, 204 from the 2010s, and 95 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most active drillers listed are Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC, associated with Phythian, Donald L., with 123 records; Heersink Drilling, associated with Heersink, Scott, with 52; and Martin, Gale, with 47. A permit history does not prove present performance. Confirm construction details, casing, grout, pump condition, and testing for the specific well being purchased.

sections.heading: What drilling a La Jara well may cost
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground identified around La Jara, the typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 120 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $6,000 to $9,000. That is the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,000 to $21,000. Use the 90th-percentile depth of 424 feet as a reminder that an ordinary bid can change substantially if the site requires a deeper hole. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical work, and any work needed to connect the system to the house.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near La Jara
sections.html:
The local well numbers are encouraging, but the records do not remove site-specific risk. A buyer should investigate low yield, an abandoned or dry hole, pump failure, poor construction, and water-quality problems. The aquifer names vary across permits, including fractured-bedrock and Confined San Luis Valley systems, so nearby wells may not behave identically even when they are close together.

Mapped environmental information is relatively clear: there are no PFAS sampling or contamination sites, historic mine features, or EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. That does not replace a laboratory water test. Check for bacteria, nitrate, metals, and other concerns appropriate to the property. Review septic setbacks, wellhead protection, drainage, access for a drilling rig, and the space needed for casing, grout, pump equipment, and electrical service.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot in the La Jara area
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction record for the exact parcel. Then inspect neighboring wells in La Jara and nearby Sanford, Manassa, Romeo, and Capulin for depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer description, use, and age. A well producing 15.0 gallons per minute is a strong local result, but the 1% of reported wells under 1 gallon per minute shows why a buyer should not skip verification.

For a new build, confirm the legal water supply before closing and identify the permitted use. Domestic or household use appears on 68% of local records, stock use on 38%, and irrigation on 9%. Exempt household-use wells are generally subject to Colorado limits, including the 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan. Have the well, septic layout, driveway, and building envelope reviewed together before committing to construction.

faq.q: How deep are wells in La Jara, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near La Jara is 120 feet. The middle half runs from 90 to 200 feet, while 58% are between 100 and 300 feet. Some are much deeper: 10% fall between 300 and 600 feet, 5% exceed 600 feet, and the deepest record is 4,000 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in La Jara?
faq.a: Typical drilling rates near La Jara are $50 to $75 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,000 to $9,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,000 to $21,000. A deeper-than-typical hole can increase the total substantially.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in La Jara?
faq.a: The median reported yield near La Jara is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 58% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Low yields are uncommon in the records, but only 151 wells report a pump yield, so the property’s own test matters.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in La Jara?
faq.a: Local well records alone cannot establish drinking-water safety. There are no mapped PFAS sites, historic mine features, or EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles, but that does not replace testing. Have the property’s water tested through a qualified laboratory, and review the well construction, septic location, casing, grout, and maintenance history.

faq.q: Should I test a well before buying land near La Jara?
faq.a: Yes. Confirm the DWR permit, construction record, depth, permitted use, pump yield, static water level, and water quality for the specific well. Local medians are 120 feet deep, 15.0 gallons per minute, and 8 feet to static water, but records vary. Also compare nearby wells in Sanford, Manassa, Romeo, and Capulin before finalizing a purchase.
